drills.title: try, catch, finally
drills.prompt: Arrange the lines into a try / catch / finally block that survives a bad amount and always says Done. Two lines do not belong.
drills.explain: The risky line goes into try. If it fails, Java jumps to the catch that matches the exception (and skips the OK line); finally runs in both cases. A catch needs a variable name after the type, and Java has no else for try blocks (that is Python).

drills.explain: throw (no s) raises one exception object now; throws only appears in a method header. catch is Java's word for Python's except, e.getMessage() gives the text the thrower wrote, and finally runs whether or not something went wrong. The first withdraw succeeds, the second one never returns a value.

drills.title: When does finally run?
drills.prompt: Read the code and type exactly what it prints, one line per line of output.
drills.explain: finally runs even when the try block has already decided to return, so "done 25" appears before main prints the 25 that parse returned. For "2x" the catch prints bad 2x, finally prints done 2x, and only then does -1 travel back to main.

drills.title: The error that was never thrown
drills.prompt: setAge(-1) should be rejected, but the program prints -1 instead. Click the faulty line, then choose the fix.
fixed_code: throw new IllegalArgumentException("Age cannot be negative");
options: throws new IllegalArgumentException("Age cannot be negative");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Age cannot be negative");
return new IllegalArgumentException("Age cannot be negative");
drills.explain: new IllegalArgumentException(...) only builds an error object. Without the word throw nothing happens, the method carries on and returns -1. throw hands the object to the nearest matching catch. throws belongs in method headers, and returning or printing the object does not stop anything.

drills.title: Review the AI's payment helpers
drills.prompt: An AI assistant wrote these helpers. They compile and run, but tick the real problems (there are three).

static int withdraw(int balance, int amount) {
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Need Rs. " + (amount - balance) + " more");
public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

issues.text: parseAmount catches every Exception and quietly returns 0
issues.why: Bad input such as "12x" turns into a payment of 0 with no trace, and real bugs (like a null text) disappear the same way. Catch NumberFormatException only, and log it or report the bad value to the caller.
Every call leaves a file handle open. Declare it in try (BufferedReader in = ...) so close() runs even when readLine fails.

issues.text: The failure is reported with System.out.println and the exception is dropped
issues.why: A log call such as LOG.log(Level.SEVERE, "could not read " + path, e) records the level, the file and the stack trace. The println loses the reason, and the LOG constant above is never used.

non_issues.why: IllegalArgumentException is unchecked, so the compiler does not require a throws clause. Documenting it is optional.

non_issues.text: Bad arguments should be reported with a checked exception
non_issues.why: IllegalArgumentException is the standard way to say "you gave me a bad value", and unchecked is the right family for it.

non_issues.text: The Logger must be created inside each method
non_issues.why: One static final Logger per class is the normal pattern and is safe to share.

drills.explain: In generated error handling look for catch blocks that hide the problem, resources opened outside try-with-resources and messages printed instead of logged.
